![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14155852/assets/d23f912d6cc6614de82fe27d1911b32fd0faa7e29bd61a9549797cfabebb3458.png)

The graphs of the functions $y=r(x)$ and $y=s(x)$ are given above. Find ${q}^{′}(3)$ where $q(x)=r(x)s(x).$
question.worked_solution:
The product rule for derivatives gives

$$
{q}^{′}(x)={r}^{′}(x)\cdot s(x)+r(x)\cdot {s}^{′}(x).
$$

As a result, we have that

$$
{q}^{′}(3)={r}^{′}(3)\cdot s(3)+r(3)\cdot {s}^{′}(3).
$$

From the graphs, we obtain that $r(3)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $s(3)=0.$

Additionally,

- The slope of $r(x)$ on $x\in (2,4)$ equals $-\frac{1}{2}.$ So, ${r}^{′}(3)=-\frac{1}{2}.$

- The slope of $s(x)$ on $x\in (2,4)$ equals $1.$ So, ${s}^{′}(3)=1.$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(3) & ={r}^{′}(3)\cdot s(3)+r(3)\cdot {s}^{′}(3) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
